title: First-Year Seminar: Learning in the Age of AI
description: An orientation to university study and to learning alongside intelligent tools. Students build durable study habits grounded in learning science, practice information literacy, examine how AI systems produce text and where they fail, and set goals for their degree.
outcomes: Explain the structure and expectations of an AIU degree and plan a sustainable study routine.
Apply evidence-based learning strategies, including retrieval practice, spacing, and interleaving.
Manage time, attention, and procrastination using self-regulation strategies.
Read actively, take useful notes, and summarize and paraphrase accurately.
Evaluate information sources, including AI-generated content, using lateral reading.
Use AI tools in ways that support learning, with transparency and academic integrity.

weeks.title: Becoming a University Student
weeks.overview: What a university education is for, how AIU courses are built, and the habits that separate students who finish from students who drift.
objectives: Describe the structure of an AIU degree, term, and course.
Explain the difference between surface learning and deep learning.
Write specific, measurable goals for your first term.
weeks.lesson:
## Why a degree, and why now?

People begin a degree for many reasons: a career change, curiosity, a promise made to themselves years ago. Whatever brought you here, it helps to name it. Researchers who study persistence in higher education consistently find that students who can articulate *why* they are studying are more likely to keep going when a course gets difficult. Your reason will not carry you through every evening of study, but it will carry you through the hard ones.

A university education is not simply a large collection of facts. It is a **sequence**. Introductory courses build the vocabulary and habits of mind that advanced courses assume. General-education courses in writing, mathematics, science, and the humanities give you breadth, so that you can think clearly about problems that do not fit neatly inside your major. And a capstone at the end asks you to put everything together.

## How AIU is organized

Every AIU bachelor's program has the same architecture:

| Unit | What it means |
|------|---------------|
| **Degree** | 4 years, 120 credit hours, 40 courses |
| **Year** | 5 terms: Fall I, Fall II, Spring I, Spring II, Summer |
| **Term** | 8 weeks, 2 courses taken together |
| **Course** | 8 weekly modules plus a cumulative final exam, worth 3 credit hours |
| **Week** | A lesson, a quiz, and a written assignment |

Because AIU is self-paced, "eight weeks" is a recommended rhythm rather than a deadline. Students who keep that rhythm finish a degree in four years. Students who need more time can take it. Students who move faster can move faster. What matters is that you keep moving.

Each week unlocks the next. To complete a week, you read the lesson, pass its quiz with at least 70 percent (you can retake quizzes as often as you like), and submit the written assignment. When all eight weeks are complete, the final exam opens. Passing it completes the course and posts a grade to your transcript.

## Surface learning versus deep learning

Educational researchers distinguish between two broad approaches to studying. **Surface learning** aims to reproduce information: memorizing definitions word for word, rereading notes until they feel familiar, cramming before a test. **Deep learning** aims to understand: asking why an idea is true, connecting it to things you already know, and testing whether you can use it in a new situation.

Surface strategies feel productive because they create a sense of familiarity. The trouble is that familiarity is not the same as understanding. You can recognize a definition when you see it and still be unable to explain it, apply it, or notice when it is being misused.

> A useful test: after reading a section, close the page and explain the main idea out loud as if to a friend. If you can't, you have learned to recognize it, not yet to know it.

This course will spend several weeks on strategies that produce deep learning, because they will pay off in every course that follows.

## Habits of students who finish

Self-paced study offers enormous freedom, and freedom cuts both ways. The students who thrive in flexible programs tend to share a few habits:

1. **They schedule study like an appointment.** "I'll study when I have time" rarely works. "I study Tuesday and Thursday from 7:00 to 8:30, and Saturday morning" usually does.
2. **They start before they feel ready.** Motivation often follows action rather than preceding it.
3. **They keep a visible record of progress.** Checking off weeks and watching a progress bar move is genuinely motivating.
4. **They ask for help early.** Confusion compounds. A concept you skip in Week 2 makes Week 4 harder.

## Setting goals that work

Vague goals ("do well this term") are hard to act on. Specific goals give you something to steer by. One common framework asks that goals be **specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, and time-bound**. Compare:

- *Vague:* "Get better at studying."
- *Specific:* "Complete one AIU week per course every eight days, studying in three scheduled sessions, through the end of this term."

The second goal tells you exactly what to do this week and lets you know whether you did it. That is the point of a good goal: not to inspire you, but to guide your next action.

## Summary

An AIU degree is a structured sequence of 40 courses delivered in eight-week terms. Success in a self-paced program depends less on talent than on habits: scheduled study, early starts, visible progress, and help-seeking. And the kind of learning that lasts is deep learning, which you will practice throughout this course.

weeks.title: How Learning Works
weeks.overview: The science of memory and the study strategies that research shows actually work: retrieval practice, spacing, interleaving, and elaboration.
objectives: Explain the roles of encoding, storage, and retrieval in learning.
Apply retrieval practice and spaced practice to your own studying.
Distinguish strategies that feel effective from strategies that are effective.
weeks.lesson:
## Learning is a change in memory

When cognitive scientists talk about learning, they usually mean a lasting change in memory that lets you do something you could not do before. Three processes are involved:

- **Encoding** turns experience into a memory trace. Paying attention, making meaning, and connecting new information to what you already know all strengthen encoding.
- **Storage** maintains that trace over time. Sleep plays an important role in consolidating new memories.
- **Retrieval** brings the memory back when you need it. Crucially, retrieving a memory does not just read it out; it *changes* it, usually making it stronger and easier to retrieve next time.

That last point is the foundation of the most useful study strategy we know of.

## Retrieval practice: the testing effect

Decades of research in laboratories and classrooms have found that practicing retrieval, by quizzing yourself or trying to recall information from memory, produces stronger long-term learning than spending the same time rereading. This is often called the **testing effect**, though "test" here means any act of pulling information out of your head.

Retrieval practice works partly because it is effortful. Struggling to recall something, even unsuccessfully, signals to your memory system that this information matters. It also reveals what you do not know, which rereading hides.

Ways to practice retrieval:

1. Close your notes and write down everything you remember about a topic, then check.
2. Turn headings into questions and answer them before reading the section.
3. Use flashcards, but say or write the answer before flipping the card.
4. Take the weekly quiz *before* you feel ready, then study what you missed.

## Spaced practice

Studying the same material in several shorter sessions spread over days produces better retention than studying it in one long session, even when the total time is identical. This is the **spacing effect**. Cramming can get you through a test tomorrow, but much of what you crammed will be gone in a few weeks, and the courses that come later in your degree assume you still have it.

A simple spacing routine: review new material the day after you learn it, again a few days later, and again the next week. Each review should be retrieval, not rereading.

## Interleaving and elaboration

**Interleaving** means mixing different kinds of problems or topics in one study session instead of practicing one type at a time. Blocked practice (ten problems of type A, then ten of type B) feels smoother, but interleaved practice teaches you to recognize *which* approach a problem calls for, which is exactly what exams and real life require.

**Elaboration** means explaining and connecting ideas: asking "why is this true?" and "how does this relate to what I learned last week?" Elaboration strengthens encoding by weaving new information into an existing web of knowledge.

## Worked example: two students, one week

Maya and Jordan each have three hours to study a lesson.

| | Maya | Jordan |
|---|---|---|
| Plan | Rereads the lesson three times on Sunday | Reads once Sunday; self-quizzes Tuesday; mixes in last week's terms Thursday |
| How it feels | Fluent, confident | Effortful, a little frustrating |
| One month later | Recognizes the terms but struggles to explain them | Can explain and apply most ideas |

Jordan's sessions felt worse and worked better. This mismatch between how studying feels and how well it works is one of the most important lessons in learning science. Researchers call strategies like Jordan's **desirable difficulties**: challenges that slow you down in the moment but improve long-term learning.

## Common misconceptions

- **"I have a learning style, so I should only study visually (or by listening)."** The popular idea that matching instruction to a preferred style improves learning has not held up well in controlled studies. Everyone benefits from combining words and visuals, and the best format depends on the material.
- **"If it feels hard, I'm doing it wrong."** Often the opposite is true.
- **"Highlighting is studying."** Highlighting can help you find key ideas, but on its own it does little for memory.

## Summary

Memory is strengthened by retrieval, spacing, interleaving, and elaboration. These strategies feel harder than rereading and cramming, which is precisely why students underuse them. Build them into your schedule and you will learn more in less time.

weeks.title: Time, Attention, and Self-Regulation
weeks.overview: Planning your weeks, protecting your attention, and understanding procrastination so that you can manage it rather than fight it.
objectives: Build a weekly study plan using time blocking.
Explain the costs of multitasking and strategies for focused work.
Describe common causes of procrastination and evidence-informed responses.
weeks.lesson:
## Self-regulated learning

In a traditional classroom, many decisions are made for you: when class meets, when assignments are due, what to do next. In a self-paced program, you make those decisions. Psychologists call the skills involved **self-regulated learning**: setting goals, planning, monitoring your progress, and adjusting your strategies. The good news is that these are skills, not traits. They improve with practice.

A useful way to think about self-regulation is as a cycle:

1. **Plan** — decide what you will do and when.
2. **Do** — carry out the plan, paying attention to how it is going.
3. **Reflect** — at the end of the week, look at what worked and what didn't.
4. **Adjust** — change the plan for next week.

## Time blocking

The most reliable way to make study happen is to give it a place on your calendar. **Time blocking** means reserving specific blocks of time for specific tasks. A block should name the task ("CS 101 Week 3: lesson and quiz"), not just the subject ("study").

A realistic AIU week for a student with a full-time job might look like this:

| Day | Block | Task |
|-----|-------|------|
| Tuesday | 7:00–8:30 pm | Course A: read lesson, take quiz |
| Thursday | 7:00–8:30 pm | Course B: read lesson, take quiz |
| Saturday | 9:00–11:30 am | Both assignments; spaced review of last week |

Notice that the Saturday block includes review. Planning time for spacing is how good intentions become habits.

## Attention is a limited resource

When people "multitask," they usually switch rapidly between tasks. Each switch carries a cost: time to reorient, and a residue of attention left on the previous task. Research on task switching consistently finds that people who switch often make more errors and take longer than when they complete tasks one at a time, even though heavy multitaskers often feel productive.

Phones are a special case. Notifications are designed to capture attention, and even the presence of a phone can be a distraction for some people. Practical steps:

- Put your phone in another room or in a drawer during study blocks.
- Close unrelated browser tabs.
- Work in focused intervals, for example 25–50 minutes, followed by a short break.
- Keep a notepad nearby to jot down intrusive to-dos so you can return to them later.

## Understanding procrastination

Procrastination is the voluntary delay of an intended action despite expecting to be worse off for the delay. It is extremely common, and it is not simply laziness. Many researchers describe it as a problem of **emotion regulation**: we put off tasks that make us feel anxious, bored, or uncertain, and the delay brings short-term relief. That relief rewards the delay, which makes it more likely next time.

Factors that make procrastination more likely include tasks that feel vague, rewards that are far away, and low confidence. That suggests responses:

- **Make the task concrete.** "Write assignment" becomes "write three sentences answering question one."
- **Shrink the first step.** Commit to just ten minutes. Starting is often the hardest part.
- **Bring rewards closer.** Track progress visibly; pair study with something pleasant, like a favorite drink.
- **Use implementation intentions.** Plans in the form "When X happens, I will do Y" ("When I finish dinner on Tuesday, I will open the Week 3 lesson") are more effective than general intentions.
- **Be kind to yourself.** Some research suggests that self-forgiveness after procrastinating reduces future procrastination, while harsh self-criticism can make the task feel even more aversive.

## Worked example: rescuing a stalled week

Sam planned to finish Week 3 of both courses by Sunday. It is Saturday, and nothing is done. Instead of abandoning the week, Sam:

1. Picks the single most important next action: the Course A lesson.
2. Sets a 25-minute timer, phone in the kitchen.
3. After the timer, takes the quiz, scores 60%, and reviews the explanations.
4. Writes a Sunday implementation intention: "After breakfast, I'll retake the quiz, then outline the assignment."

Sam doesn't finish everything, but makes real progress and, more importantly, practices restarting, which is the skill that matters most over a four-year degree.

## Common misconceptions

- **"I work best under pressure."** People often remember the last-minute successes and forget the costs. Deadlines can focus attention, but they leave no room for spacing or revision.
- **"I need to feel motivated first."** Action often creates motivation.

## Summary

Self-regulated learners plan, do, reflect, and adjust. Time blocking makes study concrete, protecting attention makes it efficient, and understanding procrastination as an emotional response makes it manageable.

weeks.title: Reading and Note-Taking for Understanding
weeks.overview: How to read academic material actively, take notes that support recall, and summarize ideas in your own words.
objectives: Use a preview–read–review process for academic reading.
Take notes in a format that supports later retrieval practice.
Write accurate summaries and paraphrases in your own words.
weeks.lesson:
## Reading is an active process

Most of your AIU coursework begins with reading a lesson. It is tempting to read the way you might read a novel, from start to finish, letting the words flow past. Academic reading works better when it is **active**: you set a purpose, ask questions, and check your understanding as you go.

## A three-stage process

**1. Preview (2–5 minutes).** Before reading closely, skim the structure. Read the overview and objectives, glance at the headings, and look at any tables or key terms. Ask: *What is this lesson trying to teach me?* Previewing builds a mental map that makes the details easier to place.

**2. Read (with questions).** Turn each heading into a question. "Spaced practice" becomes "What is spaced practice, and why does it work?" Read to answer the question. At the end of each section, pause and say the answer in your own words. If you can't, reread that section before moving on.

**3. Review (5–10 minutes).** Close the lesson and write down the main ideas from memory. Then check them against the lesson. This turns reading into retrieval practice.

This process resembles well-known methods such as SQ3R (Survey, Question, Read, Recite, Review). The names matter less than the principle: *engage before, during, and after reading.*

## Notes that work for you later

Notes serve two purposes: they help you process ideas while you learn, and they give you material to review later. Notes that simply copy the text do neither well.

### The Cornell format

One popular structure divides a page into three areas:

```
+------------------+-----------------------------------------+
|  Cues            |  Notes                                  |
|  (questions,     |  Main ideas, examples, and explanations |
|   key terms)     |  in your own words                      |
|                  |                                         |
+------------------+-----------------------------------------+
|  Summary: 2–3 sentences capturing the whole page           |
+------------------------------------------------------------+
```

While reading, you take notes in the right column. Afterward, you write questions or cue words in the left column and a short summary at the bottom. To review, cover the notes column and use the cues to quiz yourself. The format builds retrieval practice into your notes.

### Handwriting versus typing

Some studies have found that students who take notes by hand tend to process ideas more deeply because they cannot transcribe everything and must summarize. Other studies have found smaller or no differences. The more reliable lesson is about *how* you take notes: summarizing and paraphrasing beat verbatim copying regardless of the tool.

## Summarizing and paraphrasing

A **summary** condenses the main ideas of a text into a much shorter form. A **paraphrase** restates a specific passage in your own words and sentence structure, at roughly the same level of detail. Both are essential academic skills, and both must remain faithful to the original meaning.

### Worked example

> **Original:** "Retrieving a memory does not simply read it out; it changes it, usually making it stronger and easier to retrieve next time."

- **Too close (patchwriting):** "Retrieving a memory doesn't just read it out; it changes it, often making it stronger and easier to retrieve later." *(Only a few words swapped.)*
- **Good paraphrase:** "Each time we recall something, we reinforce the memory, so recalling it again becomes easier."
- **Summary of the whole lesson section:** "Recall strengthens memory, which is why self-testing is an effective study method."

A good test for paraphrasing: read the passage, close it, write your version from understanding, and then compare to make sure you kept the meaning without copying the wording. When you use someone else's ideas in an assignment, you still credit the source, even when the words are your own. You will practice this formally in College Composition.

## Common misconceptions

- **"More notes are better notes."** Notes that capture everything often capture nothing in particular. Aim for main ideas, examples, and your own questions.
- **"Changing a few words makes it my own."** Patchwriting keeps the original structure and is not a true paraphrase.

## Summary

Active reading means previewing, reading with questions, and reviewing from memory. Notes are most useful when they are in your own words and built for later self-testing. Summaries and paraphrases must be faithful to the source and genuinely your own.

keyTerms.definition: Reading with a purpose, asking questions, and checking understanding throughout.
A note format with cue, notes, and summary areas designed for self-testing.
A condensed statement of a text's main ideas.
A restatement of a passage in your own words and structure, faithful to its meaning.
Copying a source's structure while swapping a few words; not an acceptable paraphrase.

quiz.explanation: Covering the notes and answering cues turns review into retrieval practice.

quiz.explanation: A paraphrase is faithful and genuinely rewritten; a much shorter version covering the whole text is a summary.

quiz.prompt: What is the most reliable conclusion about note-taking?
choices: Summarizing in your own words is more effective than verbatim copying

quiz.explanation: How you process information matters more than the tool you use.

weeks.title: Information Literacy
weeks.overview: Finding, evaluating, and using information well in a world where anyone can publish anything, including machines.
objectives: Distinguish primary, secondary, and tertiary sources.
Evaluate a source using lateral reading and the SIFT moves.
Explain why peer review matters and what it does not guarantee.
weeks.lesson:
## Why information literacy matters

**Information literacy** is the ability to recognize when you need information and to find, evaluate, and use it effectively and ethically. It has always been a core academic skill. Today it is also a survival skill: search engines, social media, and AI tools can all deliver confident-sounding answers that are partly or entirely wrong.

## Types of sources

| Type | What it is | Examples |
|------|------------|----------|
| **Primary** | Original evidence or first-hand accounts | A research study reporting its own experiment, a historical letter, raw data, an interview |
| **Secondary** | Analysis or interpretation of primary sources | A review article, a textbook chapter, a documentary, a news analysis |
| **Tertiary** | Summaries and indexes of other sources | Encyclopedias, dictionaries, databases |

None of these is automatically "better." Primary sources give you direct evidence but may require expertise to interpret. Secondary sources provide context. Tertiary sources are excellent starting points but rarely the right thing to cite in academic work.

## Scholarly sources and peer review

In academic work you will often be asked to use **peer-reviewed** sources. Peer review is a process in which experts in a field evaluate a research article before a journal publishes it. Reviewers check whether the methods are sound, the conclusions follow from the evidence, and the work contributes something new.

Peer review is valuable, but it is not a guarantee of truth. Reviewers can miss errors, and individual studies can fail to replicate. A single study is a data point; a consistent body of research is much stronger evidence. Good scholars pay attention to the weight of evidence, not just the existence of a study.

## Lateral reading

How do professional fact-checkers evaluate an unfamiliar website? Researchers who studied this question found that experts behave very differently from most students. Students tended to read **vertically**: staying on the page, examining its design, its "About" section, and its own claims. Fact-checkers read **laterally**: they quickly left the page and opened new tabs to see what *other* sources said about the site and its claims.

Lateral reading works because a source's description of itself is the least reliable information about it. Polished design and official-sounding names are easy to fake.

## The SIFT moves

A widely taught set of habits, developed for quickly evaluating online information, is summarized as **SIFT**:

1. **Stop.** Before you share or rely on something, pause. Do you know this source? What is your purpose?
2. **Investigate the source.** Read laterally to learn who is behind it and what their expertise and motives are.
3. **Find better coverage.** Look for trusted reporting or research on the same claim. Is there a consensus?
4. **Trace claims to their original context.** Quotes, images, and statistics are often stripped of context. Find where they first appeared.

### Worked example

You see a post: *"New study proves that studying with music boosts test scores by 40%!"* Applying SIFT:

- **Stop:** A dramatic number and the word "proves" are warning signs.
- **Investigate:** The post comes from a company that sells "focus music" subscriptions. That is a potential conflict of interest.
- **Find better coverage:** Searching for research on background music and studying shows mixed findings; effects depend on the person, the task, and the music (lyrics tend to interfere with reading).
- **Trace:** The original study, once found, involved a small sample, measured mood rather than test scores, and did not claim a 40% gain.

Conclusion: the claim misrepresents its source.

## Information from AI tools

AI chatbots can be helpful for explaining ideas, but they generate text by predicting likely words, not by looking up verified facts (you will learn more about this next week). They can produce plausible but false statements, including citations to articles that do not exist. Treat AI output as you would an unsourced claim from a knowledgeable acquaintance: potentially useful, never authoritative on its own, and always worth verifying with SIFT. This applies to AIU's own AI-written lessons, too.

## Common misconceptions

- **".org sites are trustworthy."** Anyone can register a .org domain.
- **"If it's peer-reviewed, it's settled."** Peer review is a filter, not a final verdict.
- **"I can judge a site by how professional it looks."** Design says little about accuracy.

## Summary

Information-literate learners know what kind of source they are looking at, read laterally rather than taking a source's word for itself, and trace claims back to their origins. These habits apply equally to websites, social media, research articles, and AI.

weeks.title: How AI Language Models Work
weeks.overview: A plain-language look inside the AI systems that write text, including the ones that wrote this course: what they are, how they are trained, and why they make mistakes.
objectives: Explain at a high level how a large language model generates text.
Describe the main stages of training a modern AI assistant.
Identify typical strengths and failure modes of language models, including hallucination.
weeks.lesson:
## A word about this lesson

AIU's courses are written by AI models. It seems only fair that you understand what those systems are. This lesson is a non-technical overview; if you go on to study computer science, you'll learn the mathematics in courses like Machine Learning Foundations and Artificial Intelligence.

## Predicting the next word

A **large language model (LLM)** is a computer program that has learned statistical patterns in enormous amounts of text. At its core, it does one thing: given some text, it predicts what is likely to come next. Technically it works with **tokens**, which are chunks of text such as words or pieces of words.

To write a paragraph, the model predicts a likely next token, adds it to the text, and repeats, thousands of times. When you ask a chatbot a question, your question becomes the beginning of a text, and the model continues it with what a helpful answer would plausibly look like.

This sounds simple, but predicting text well turns out to require a great deal. To predict the next word in a chemistry explanation, a legal argument, or a line of computer code, a model benefits from representing grammar, facts, reasoning patterns, and the structure of arguments. Modern models are surprisingly capable as a result, and researchers continue to study exactly how they represent what they have learned.

## How models are trained

Training a modern AI assistant typically involves several stages:

1. **Pretraining.** The model is shown vast amounts of text and repeatedly adjusts billions of internal numerical values, called **parameters**, to get better at predicting the next token. This stage gives the model broad knowledge and language ability.
2. **Fine-tuning.** The model is further trained on examples of helpful conversations, such as answering questions or following instructions.
3. **Learning from feedback.** People (and sometimes other AI systems guided by written principles) compare different responses, and the model is trained to prefer responses judged more helpful, honest, and harmless.

The model does not store its training text like a library of documents to look things up in. Its knowledge is spread across its parameters in a way that is more like a compressed, blurry impression of what it read.

## Strengths

Language models are often very good at:

- Explaining concepts in different ways and at different levels.
- Summarizing, outlining, and reorganizing text.
- Drafting writing and code in many styles.
- Answering questions about widely discussed topics.
- Following detailed instructions about format and tone.

## Failure modes

Because a model generates *plausible* text rather than retrieving *verified* facts, it can fail in characteristic ways:

- **Hallucination (confabulation):** stating false information confidently, such as inventing a statistic, a quotation, or a citation to an article that does not exist.
- **Knowledge cutoffs:** a model trained on data up to a certain date may not know about later events unless it is connected to a search tool.
- **Reasoning slips:** errors in arithmetic or multi-step logic, especially when it answers quickly.
- **Sensitivity to phrasing:** slightly different questions can produce different answers.
- **Sycophancy:** a tendency to agree with the user or tell people what they seem to want to hear.
- **Bias:** patterns in training data, including social biases, can show up in outputs.

### Worked example: a fabricated source

A student asks a chatbot for "three peer-reviewed studies on spaced practice with citations." The model produces three neat citations with authors, titles, journals, and years. Two are real; one combines a real author's name with a title that sounds right but was never published. Nothing in the text signals which is which. The only way to know is to check, using the lateral reading skills from last week.

## What this means for you as a learner

- Use AI to explain, quiz, and give feedback, but verify facts that matter.
- Be especially skeptical of specific numbers, quotations, and citations.
- Ask the model to show its reasoning, and check the steps.
- Remember that fluent, confident writing is not evidence of accuracy.

The same applies to this course. AIU's lessons are checked for structure and consistency, but AI-written material can still contain errors. If something seems wrong, investigate it. Noticing an error in a lesson is a sign you are learning, not a failure.

## Common misconceptions

- **"The AI looks up answers on the internet."** Unless connected to a search tool, it generates from patterns learned in training.
- **"If it sounds confident, it's probably right."** Confidence of tone is not tied to accuracy.
- **"It's just autocomplete, so it can't do anything impressive."** Next-token prediction at scale produces capabilities that are genuinely useful, along with real limits.

## Summary

Large language models generate text by repeatedly predicting likely next tokens, using patterns learned during training. They are powerful tools for explanation and drafting, but they can produce fluent falsehoods. Understanding how they work is the first step to using them well.

keyTerms.definition: An AI system trained on large amounts of text to predict likely continuations of text.
A unit of text, such as a word or part of a word, that a language model processes.
The internal numerical values a model adjusts during training.
The initial training stage in which a model learns to predict text from a large corpus.
When an AI model states false information, such as an invented citation, as if it were true.

choices: Using it to explain and quiz you, while verifying important facts

quiz.explanation: AI can support learning, but factual claims need verification.

weeks.title: Using AI Tools Responsibly
weeks.overview: Academic integrity in the age of AI: the difference between using AI to learn and using it to avoid learning, plus privacy and transparency.
objectives: Explain the purpose of academic integrity and why it matters for your own learning.
Distinguish AI uses that support learning from uses that replace it.
Apply guidelines for transparency, verification, and privacy when using AI.
weeks.lesson:
## What academic integrity protects

**Academic integrity** means honesty and responsibility in scholarly work: doing your own work, giving credit to others, and representing your knowledge truthfully. Rules against plagiarism and cheating can seem like hurdles, but they protect something valuable: the link between your credential and what you actually know.

At AIU, that link matters even more than usual. AIU's credentials are not accredited degrees. Their entire value is the learning they represent. If you outsource an assignment, you lose the only thing the assignment was for.

## A tutor, not a ghostwriter

AI tools can support learning remarkably well, or they can quietly replace it. A helpful question to ask is: *Is the AI doing the thinking this assignment is meant to build in me?*

| Supports learning | Replaces learning |
|-------------------|-------------------|
| Asking for a different explanation of a confusing concept | Asking it to write your assignment |
| Having it quiz you on the week's key terms | Pasting quiz questions in to get answers |
| Asking for feedback on a draft you wrote | Submitting its rewrite as your own work |
| Brainstorming questions to explore | Accepting its argument without evaluating it |
| Checking your solution after you've attempted a problem | Asking for the solution before trying |

Notice that the same tool appears in both columns. What differs is *who does the cognitive work*. Learning requires effort; when you hand the effort to a machine, you also hand it the learning.

## A practical framework

When you use AI in your studies, follow four habits:

1. **Attempt first.** Try the problem, draft the paragraph, or recall the concept before asking for help. Then AI feedback has something to work on, and you will remember more.
2. **Verify.** Treat factual claims, numbers, and sources as unconfirmed until you check them.
3. **Be transparent.** If AI meaningfully shaped work you submit, say how. Many instructors and employers now expect a brief note such as "I used an AI assistant to suggest a clearer structure for my second paragraph."
4. **Protect privacy.** Don't paste sensitive personal information, confidential work documents, or other people's private data into AI tools without understanding how that data will be stored and used.

## AIU's own use of AI

AIU uses AI to write course materials and, where enabled, to give feedback on written assignments against the published rubric. We think you deserve to know that, which is why it is noted on each course. AI feedback can be useful for revision, but it can also be wrong. If feedback seems mistaken, compare it carefully against the rubric and the lesson.

## Worked example: three students, one assignment

The assignment asks students to explain how retrieval practice could improve their study habits.

- **Ana** asks an AI to write the essay and submits it. She receives credit but has learned nothing about retrieval practice, and the essay doesn't reflect her actual habits.
- **Ben** writes his own draft, then asks an AI: "What is the weakest part of my argument?" He considers the feedback, revises one paragraph in his own words, and notes the help in a sentence at the end.
- **Cara** writes the essay without AI, then uses an AI to quiz her on the week's terms before the next lesson.

Ben and Cara both used AI responsibly. Ana's choice cost her the learning, and in many institutions would be treated as academic dishonesty.

## Common misconceptions

- **"If AI wrote it, no one was plagiarized."** Submitting work you didn't produce as your own misrepresents your learning, regardless of the source.
- **"Using AI at all is cheating."** Many uses support learning. The question is how, and whether you're transparent.
- **"AI detectors can reliably catch AI writing."** Detection tools are known to be unreliable and can produce false positives. Integrity is better built on honest practice than on surveillance.

## Summary

Academic integrity protects the connection between your work and your learning. Use AI as a tutor: attempt first, verify claims, be transparent about meaningful help, and protect private information. The goal is not to avoid AI, but to stay the author of your own education.

weeks.title: Your Path Forward
weeks.overview: Bringing it together: mindset, resilience, and a plan for the next four years of your degree.
objectives: Explain how beliefs about ability can influence persistence.
Develop strategies for setbacks and sustaining motivation over a long program.
Create a personal learning plan for your degree.
weeks.lesson:
## Looking back

Over seven weeks you have studied how AIU works, how memory works, how to manage time and attention, how to read and take notes, how to evaluate information, how AI language models work, and how to use them responsibly. This final week asks you to turn those ideas into a plan for the long journey ahead.

## Beliefs about ability

Psychologist Carol Dweck and colleagues have described two contrasting beliefs people can hold about ability. In a **fixed mindset**, abilities like intelligence are seen as largely unchangeable. In a **growth mindset**, abilities are seen as capable of development through effort, good strategies, and help from others.

The idea became enormously popular, and later research has added important nuance. Large studies have found that brief growth-mindset interventions tend to have modest average effects on grades, with larger benefits for some groups, such as students who were struggling. A growth mindset is also easy to misunderstand: it is not simply praising effort, and it is not a belief that anyone can do anything instantly. The useful core is this: **when you struggle, the struggle is information about what to practice next, not a verdict on who you are.**

## Setbacks are part of the plan

Over 40 courses, you will have weeks when life intervenes, quizzes you fail several times, and topics that feel impossible at first. Planning for setbacks in advance makes them easier to handle:

- **Normalize them.** Nearly every student who completes a degree has a story about a term that went badly.
- **Diagnose, don't judge.** Was the problem time, strategy, prerequisite knowledge, or something outside your control? Each points to a different fix.
- **Have a restart ritual.** For example: review your goals, pick the smallest next step, and do it within 24 hours.
- **Use your strategies.** When a course gets hard, return to retrieval practice, spacing, and active reading. Hard material is where they help most.

## Sustaining motivation over four years

Motivation researchers often distinguish **intrinsic motivation** (doing something because it is interesting or meaningful) from **extrinsic motivation** (doing something for an outside reward, like a credential or a raise). Both are legitimate, and most students have both. Over a long program, intrinsic motivation tends to be more durable, so it helps to cultivate it:

- Connect each course to your goals or interests, even when the connection takes some thought.
- Notice your own progress, which supports a sense of **competence**.
- Make choices where you can, such as electives and capstone topics, which supports a sense of **autonomy**.
- Find people to share your learning with, which supports a sense of **connection**.

These three needs, competence, autonomy, and relatedness, are central to self-determination theory, one of the most widely studied frameworks in motivation psychology.

## Reading your degree map

Open your program's degree map. Notice its shape:

- **Year 1** builds foundations: writing, mathematics, and introductory courses in your major.
- **Year 2** develops the core of your field alongside breadth in general education.
- **Year 3** moves into advanced, specialized courses.
- **Year 4** adds electives and culminates in a capstone where you apply everything.

Look ahead at the courses that excite you most and the ones that worry you. Both are useful to know now.

## Worked example: a personal learning plan

Here is part of one student's plan:

> **Long-term goal:** Complete the B.S. in Business Administration within five years, studying about eight hours a week.
>
> **This year:** Finish Year 1 (10 courses). Study Tuesday and Thursday evenings and Saturday mornings.
>
> **Strategies I'll keep:** Self-quiz before each weekly quiz; Cornell notes; Sunday 15-minute weekly review.
>
> **Likely obstacle:** Busy season at work in December. **Plan:** Drop to one course-week per week rather than stopping completely.
>
> **Why it matters:** I want to move into management and prove to myself that I can finish this.

Notice how specific it is, and how it plans for difficulty rather than assuming smooth sailing.

## Summary

Treat struggle as information, plan for setbacks, nurture the motivation that will last, and keep your plan specific. You now have the strategies most students never learn explicitly. Use them, and the next 39 courses will be easier for it.
